newsitem.title: USA: Japanese prime minister's remarks boost dollar.
newsitem.headline: Japanese prime minister's remarks boost dollar.

text.p: NEW YORK, Feb 3 - The dollar rose Monday against the Japanese yen and German mark after Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said leading industrial nations are unlikely to join forces to weaken the U.S. currency.
Hashimoto told a Japanese parliamentary committee that the dollar is unlikely to be lowered through international cooperation, even though excessive strengthening of the currency was undesirable.
"It helped the dollar," said Diego Giurleo, at Royal Bank of Canada. "He's basically saying there is going to be no concerted intervention to bring the dollar down."

Since falling to a post-World War II low of 1.3438 German marks on March 8, 1995, and 79.75 Japanese yen on April 19 of the same year, the dollar has risen nearly 24 percent against the mark and more than 50 percent vs. the yen.

Senior financial officials of the Group of Seven major industrial powers -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- helped to engineer the sharp dollar gains after the currency hit bottom in 1995.
Currency traders are eagerly watching for any clues about whether these officials will decide the dollar rally has gone far enough when they meet again in Berlin on Saturday.
Hashimoto's remarks were made overnight in Tokyo, and the dollar hit its peak for the day as trading got under way in New York. It climbed briefly to 1.6490 marks and 122.24 yen.
In late New York trading, the dollar fetched 1.6400 marks and 121.70 yen, up from 1.6387 marks and 121.43 yen Friday.
The pound rose to $1.6197 from $1.6020 on Friday. The dollar also fell to 1.4180 Swiss francs from 1.4239 francs, and to Canadian $1.3443 from C$1.3472.
On Tuesday and Wednesday, the Federal Open Market Committee, the Federal Reserve's policy arm, meets to decide the future course of short-term interest rates.

Most analysts predict the policy-makers will leave rates unchanged. The last time the committee altered rates was on Jan. 31, 1996, when it cut two key short-term rates in a bid to stimulate economic growth. Any announcement on rates is expected Wednesday.

Expectations are for unchanged monetary policy, said Bob Lynch, a senior currency analyst at MMS International. "You may see some tail-off in activity just in case the Fed surprises (the market) with a move," he said.
